claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 develops several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases during slower cooling.
The untreated alloy exhibits extensive, multistep primary crystallization after rapid and slower cooling.
A high-energy pulsed-laser quenching step after slower cooling will suppress primary nucleation.
Pulsed-laser quenching will increase the stability and retention of the amorphous phase.
The laser pulse should be applied during the early stage of reheating following moderate cooling.
The laser-induced local cooling rate should substantially exceed 10^6 K/s.
The laser pulse locally remelts surface regions.
Rapid localized remelting and quenching minimizes or eradicates pre-existing crystalline nuclei.
Ultrahigh-rate quenching kinetically hinders nucleation and growth of primary crystalline phases.
Removal of pre-existing nuclei produces a more homogeneous amorphous structure.
Having fewer crystalline nuclei delays crystallization during subsequent reheating.
Laser-treated samples will have a higher amorphous fraction than untreated samples.
Laser-treated samples will exhibit an elevated apparent glass-formation temperature.
Laser-treated samples will exhibit a delayed or reduced crystallization exotherm during thermal analysis.
The treatment benefit requires localized cooling above approximately 10^6 K/s and subsequent reheating below the crystallization onset.
Insufficient laser energy, inappropriate pulse duration, or reheating above the critical temperature may prevent crystallization suppression.
Optimal laser energy density and pulse duration depend on sample thickness and local thermal conductivity.
A surface laser treatment may not scale straightforwardly to bulk amorphous retention.
